extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys, and applicants in ASEAN Member States (AMS)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for assessing patentability in AMS: determining novelty (including ranges and selection inventions), second medical use claims, prior art (including internet/implicit disclosures), and inventive step (problem-solution and Windsurfing tests) from the perspective of a Person Skilled in the Art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of numerical ranges / sub-ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention that selects a narrower sub-range of numerical values within a broader known range may be novel if the selected sub-range has not been explicitly mentioned in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish the novelty of the sub-range, the selected sub-range should be narrow and sufficiently specific from the known broader range, illustrated by means of examples. The interpretation of 'sufficient specificity' is key and may vary on the facts of the case; novelty must be decided on a case-by-case basis. If the claimed range merely falls within the broader range without sufficient specificity, anticipation may occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior-art borders on range novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior-art document discloses the two borders of a numerical range, those borders may destroy novelty for claimed subject-matter that contains one of the borders when features have discontinuous numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the technical features are any numbers between the two borders, the prior-art borders may not destroy novelty. Assess on the numerical/technical facts of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-art teaching very close to claimed range does not anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art which teaches a value or range very close to, but not overlapping or touching, the claimed range does not anticipate the claimed range; the claimed subject matter is novel in that situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive step still needs to be determined. Some AMS (e.g., Viet Nam) provide specific criteria when a claimed numerical range is 'close' to a specific prior-art number: (a) the claimed range is sufficiently far removed from any specific number disclosed; (b) the claimed range is narrow compared to the specific number; (c) the claimed range provides an effect that makes the claimed subject matter 'special' (e.g., particular technical effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection invention / narrow-range unexpected results
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to a narrow range and the prior art discloses a broad range, the narrow range may be novel if it is not merely one way of carrying out the prior-art teaching and there is evidence (e.g., unexpected results) that the advantageous effect occurs only within the claimed narrow range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unexpected results that occur with high probability only within the claimed range may render the claims unobvious as well as novel (selection invention). Consider all relevant facts of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requires sufficient specificity in prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: To anticipate a claim, the claimed subject matter should be disclosed with sufficient specificity in the item of prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sufficient specificity is interpreted case-by-case; mere proximity or closeness of numbers is not necessarily anticipation. The examiner must evaluate whether prior art discloses the claimed subject matter with the necessary detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second medical use claim formats and patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to new medical uses of known medicines (second medical use) are treated differently across AMS; certain claim formats are acceptable while others are excluded as methods of treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A claim in the form 'Use of substance X for the treatment of disease Y' may be regarded as a method of treatment excluded from patentability in some AMS. A claim in the form 'Product X for use in the treatment of disease Y' can be patentable (subject to national exceptions). Swiss-type or 'manufacture of a medicament' formulations are often used to claim second medical uses. Some jurisdictions (e.g., Philippines) require Swiss-type format or enhanced efficacy for derivatives (salts, polymorphs, etc.). Singapore and Malaysia permit 'Substance X for use in treatment Y' or 'Use of compound X in the manufacture of a medicament for the treatment of disease Y' where the use is new and inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/inventive-step assessment difference for second medical uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Second medical use claims can derive novelty from the specified medical use if that use is new and inventive, even where the substance itself is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some AMS exclude claims that apply the product into a subject's body or involve dosage/efficacy in the claim; acceptable formats avoid direct method-of-treatment language. National laws may further limit second use claims (e.g., Indonesia's Article 4(f) excluding new uses that do not show significant efficiency increase).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art definition for novelty and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art is everything made available to the public anywhere in the world before the relevant date (filing or priority date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes written disclosure, oral disclosure, prior use and sale, irrespective of geographical location, language, or age. For obviousness analysis, unpublished patent applications with earlier priority dates are to be disregarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet and online disclosures as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures on the internet or in online databases are treated the same as other written disclosures for prior-art purposes; a website can be prior art even if access is restricted or payment is required, provided there is no bar of confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing publication dates may be difficult; where dates are present they are generally accepted at face value and the burden is on the applicant to rebut them. Different online sources have differing reliability (scientific publishers, academic institutions, standards bodies are highly reliable). Computer-generated timestamps and 'last modified' dates can be considered reliable unless there are indications to the contrary. For disclosures with no date or unreliable date, further information should be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner obligation when publication date is contested
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant contests the public availability or assumed publication date of a cited document, the examiner must consider whether to investigate further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant shows sound reasons to doubt that the document forms part of the state of the art and further investigation does not produce sufficient evidence to remove that doubt, the examiner should not pursue the matter further. The examiner must present evidence to maintain a disputed publication date if continuing to rely on it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit (inherent) disclosure counts as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure may be implicit in a prior-art document; such implicit teachings can be considered part of the prior art and can destroy novelty or inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the implicit teaching would have been directly and unambiguously derivable by the PSIA from the prior-art disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step (non-obviousness) general test
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention involves an inventive step if, having regard to the prior art, it is not obvious at the relevant date to a Person Skilled in the Art (PSIA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty must be established before inventive step is considered. For inventive step it is permissible to make a 'mosaic' of prior art provided the combination could be made by an unimaginative PSIA with no inventive capacity. The relevant date is the filing date or priority date as applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider claimed invention as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing inventive step, the claimed invention must be considered as a whole rather than merely examining whether individual differences would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, where the claim is merely an 'aggregation or juxtaposition of features' and not a true combination producing a synergistic effect, it may be sufficient to show the individual features are obvious. Account should also be taken of what the applicant acknowledges as known in the description and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider prior arts as a whole and motivation to combine
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior arts must be considered in their entirety and the PSIA must be motivated or prompted to combine teachings of the prior arts to arrive at the claimed subject-matter, including consideration of a reasonable expectation or likelihood of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the prior art and common general knowledge would have provided sufficient motivation for the PSIA to combine or modify prior teachings to reach the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impermissible hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior arts and the assessment of inventive step must be viewed without the benefit of hindsight afforded by the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should avoid ex post facto analysis; when combining documents from a search they should visualize the overall prior art confronting the PSIA before the applicant's contribution, and make a 'real-life' assessment giving fair weight to applicant arguments and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Person Skilled in the Art (PSIA) definition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: The PSIA is a hypothetical person having common general knowledge in the relevant art at the relevant date and the ability to use ordinary technical means and ordinary creativity (selecting materials, optimising ranges, substituting equivalents, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PSIA standard sets a floor and ceiling for obviousness: average/ordinary skill is assumed (extraordinary skill is excluded). Consider field-specific knowledge and common general knowledge when assessing what the PSIA would have done.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-solution approach (method for determining inventive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: A three-step test: (i) determine the closest prior art; (ii) establish the objective technical problem to be solved; (iii) consider whether the claimed invention starting from the closest prior art and the objective technical problem would have been obvious to the PSIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closest prior art is the single reference that is the most promising starting point (same field or problem, most features in common, similar use, fewest modifications). The objective technical problem is derived objectively from differences between the claimed invention and closest prior art and may be reformulated based on facts found in examination; it can be an aggregation of partial problems if multiple technical effects exist. In stage three, the examiner asks whether prior art teachings would have 'prompted' the PSIA to reach the claimed invention (not merely that they 'could' have).

rubrics_metrics.name: Windsurfing / Pozzoli test (alternative obviousness method)
rubrics_metrics.description: A four-step test (Windsurfing as adapted in Pozzoli): (1) identify the notional PSIA and common general knowledge; (2) identify the inventive concept of the claim or construe it; (3) identify differences between the prior art and the inventive concept; (4) decide, without knowledge of the invention, whether these differences would have been obvious to the PSIA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This test does not require identification of the 'closest prior art' but requires evaluation of whether differences require any degree of invention. Use the Pozzoli restatement where appropriate.
